episodes.214246: During the 27th afternoon and evening, a warm unstable air mass interacting with an upper wave and associated surface boundary developed scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Convection initiated around 15:27 EST over northern portions of central Indiana and overspread locations further south before diminishing during the evening hours.||Severe thunderstorm wind gusts were the primary hazard, with peak gusts estimated and measured between 58 mph and 60 mph. Official surface observations included a 58 mph gust recorded by the Muncie ASOS (KMIE) in Delaware County and a 59 mph gust at the Indianapolis ASOS (KIND) in Marion County. Wind damage was scattered across most eastern counties and a couple western zones, with numerous downed trees and powerlines, snapped utility poles and localized structural damage. Hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter was reported in Marion and Warren county, with broken windows in Warren county from wind-driven hail.||Additionally, torrential rainfall of 1.20-2.00 inches in approximately 30 minutes resulted in localized flash flooding in Marion County between 17:00 and 21:00 EST. Rapid runoff inundated low-lying roadways, stranded or partially submerged multiple vehicles in high water, and caused localized yard and basement flooding.

episodes.214450: Showers and thunderstorms stationed across central Pennsylvania and southern New York during the late evening hours of July 27, 2026 continued to exhibit signs of strengthening as they continued into July 28th. This trend was due to there being sufficient instability for storms to continue to sustain themselves as they continued overnight into the 28th. A severe thunderstorm north of the Pennsylvania-New York border moved south of the border during the late evening hours and produced a severe wind gust at Bradford Regional Airport; however, no damage was observed with this storm. Similarly, a severe thunderstorm stationed across central Pennsylvania moves southward into Adams County, where tree damage was observed during the early morning hours of July 28th. Winds parallel to storm motion allowed for multiple rounds of heavy rainfall for locations, with considerable flash flooding beginning during the morning hours of July 28th in McKean County. The communities of Eldred and Lewis Run were hit especially hard with flooding with multiple businesses and multiple roadways taking on over one foot of water. As these storms shifted southward, similarly flooding was observed in the town of Coalport, where multiple streets were under one foot of water and there were reported water rescues in the town due to stranded cars during the early afternoon hours. Breaks in the cloud deck occurred further southeast during the morning and early afternoon hours, allowing for thunderstorms to become strong-to-severe quickly across the southern tier of Pennsylvania, where multiple instances of tree damage were observed in Cumberland, Dauphin, York, Adams, and Franklin Counties. Due to saturated soils, isolated instances of flash flooding was observed in Lebanon County along with more widespread flooding in the town of Waynesboro in Franklin County where multiple roadways were closed due to rising water.

episodes.216013: During the early morning hours of July 28, 2026, a thunderstorm complex pushing across southeast Nebraska brought damaging wind gusts and flash flooding to Lancaster County. The system was forced by a shortwave trough pushing into a modestly unstable airmass with sufficient bulk shear to support strong to severe storms. Radar trends indicate the thunderstorm complex, which initially developed over south-central Nebraska, tracked eastward into southeast Nebraska during the early morning hours.||While base velocity radar scans displayed strong winds above the surface across Seward and Saline counties, these winds mixed down to the surface as the complex moved across Lancaster County. This resulted in several reports of downed trees and large branches in Lincoln, NE, alongside a 58 mph wind gust recorded by the KLNK ASOS at the Lincoln Municipal Airport around 1:20 AM CST.||The thunderstorms were also efficient rainfall producers, generating precipitation rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and quickly dropping 2 to 4 inches of total rainfall. Consequently, a law enforcement report out of Lincoln confirmed multiple flooded streets, several stranded vehicles, and one water rescue at 2:00 AM CST. The severe threat gradually decreased in intensity as the storms progressed eastward into the mid-morning hours.

episodes.216684: An unprecedented heavy rain event/rain storm impacted eastern NY and western New England on July 28-30, 2026. Scattered to numerous instances of flash flooding occurred with the Greater Capital Region, eastern Catskills and northern portions of the mid-Hudson Valley being the hardest hit. A closed/cutoff low was positioned over the region. The mid and upper low captured a double-barrel low pressure system with one low centered over eastern/southern NY and a secondary coastal low southeast of Long Island. Meso-vortices migrated around the mid and upper level low over the region. A tremendous fetch of deep moisture occurred from the Atlantic and Gulf. Precipitable water anomalies were 2-3 standard deviations above normal in the 1.40-1.80 inch range. Freezing levels were high in the 11-13 kft above ground level range.  Very efficient rainfall processes occurred with more of a cool season style synoptic system with an impressive stratiform rainband with initially embedded convection in the low/mid level deformation zone of the system. Intense rainfall rates of 1-3 inches per hour and thunderstorms/heavy showers repeatedly moved over the same areas. The Greater Capital Region, northern reaches of the mid-Hudson Valley and eastern Catskills received the most rainfall with widespread amounts of 6 to 12 inches.||Impressive, record-breaking rainfall amounts occurred in a 2-day stretch, though most of the rainfall occurred in a 24-30 hour period. 5.45 inches of rain occurred on July 29th at Albany, shattering the old record of 1.90 inches set in 1974. This was also the wettest July day on record for Albany. This calendar day total is the 2nd wettest day on record overall, only behind the 5.60 inches that occurred on Sept 16, 1999 with TS Floyd moisture. The 2-day total at Albany was 7.00 inches.||The NYS Mesonet network recorded 11.79 inches of rainfall at Schodack and 11.47 inches at Kinderhook.  This was a 1 in a 1000 year precipitation/heavy rain event for those areas. Poughkeepsie also had 2.68 of rainfall on July 29th which broke the old record of 1.86 in 1971.||Despite this much rainfall, abnormally dry conditions ahead of this event limited impacts from river flooding. Only five river points reached flood stage (4 Minor and one Moderate) during this event with one river falling just short of minor flood stage (Mt Marion on the Esopus).
episodes.216700: An area of low pressure slowly moving across the region, along with an associated frontal boundary and supporting upper energy, brought multiple rounds of showers and embedded strong thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall. The slow-moving nature of the convection combined with strong mid level winds, also known as a low level jet, enhancing moisture and lift, especially over the Catskills, resulted in rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches and widespread flash flooding across Sullivan County.

episodes.216890: On July 28th, the Weather Prediction Center designated portions of Western and Central New York under an Excessive Rainfall Outlook (ERO) as a tropical-moisture-laden air mass overspread the region. Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo highlighted precipitable water values well above average, providing the ambient fuel for torrential downpours with high hourly rainfall rates. Slow-moving convective storm clusters developed during the morning and early afternoon, dropping 1 to 2+ inches of rain per hour over parts of Erie, Livingston, and neighboring counties. Consequently, NWS Buffalo issued Flash Flood Warnings as the intense rainfall rates overwhelmed local drainage systems, resulting in rapid urban runoff, inundated roadways, and low-lying street flooding across the metro area.
episodes.216891: On July 27th, 2026, the Storm Prediction Center highlighted a severe weather risk across Western and Central New York as a dynamic shortwave trough tracked across the Great Lakes into an unstable air mass. Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo detailed that strong daytime surface heating combined with elevated low-level moisture to build moderate afternoon CAPE across the region. Convective initiation occurred along afternoon lake breezes and pre-frontal convergence lines before tracking eastward across the Genesee Valley and Finger Lakes. The primary severe weather hazards observed were localized damaging straight-line wind gusts that downed isolated tree limbs and power lines, accompanied by frequent cloud-to-ground lightning and heavy downpours.

episodes.217004: Over much of the end of July, including on July 26th and 27th, a persistent northwest flow mid- and upper-level pattern set up from the Great Lakes down into the Tennessee Valley. This allowed a series of mesoscale convective systems to drop from north to south across the region, each of which brought strong to severe thunderstorms with swaths of damaging winds to the Ohio Valley. On July 26th, a cluster of storms initiated over southwest Indiana and southern Illinois during the afternoon hours before pushing to the south-southeast into western and south central Kentucky. While the most potent portion of this complex impacted areas just to the west of the NWS Louisville warning area, a few instances of wind damage were observed as the complex of storms moved across the Cave region of south central Kentucky. On July 27th, the pattern shifted to the north and east across the region, bringing the main storm track into southeast Indiana and the Bluegrass region of Kentucky. An MCS descending from central Indiana would produce scattered wind damage as it moved across the area, with a smattering of tree damage and a few wind gusts exceeding 60 mph observed.

NWS storm survey found the path of an EF-0 tornado that touched down in the Allegheny community. Initial tree damage, consisting of broken large branches and a few uprooted or partially snapped trees was first observed along Rock Branch Rd near the intersection of Highway 212. The tornado tracked southeast across Highway 212, with the most concentrated area of damage observed along the southward-facing slope of Shelton Laurel Creek, where numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. The tornado continued southeast to Cutshall Town Rd, where several pine trees were snapped. Additional broken branches and a few uprooted trees were noted in a distant wooded area looking back toward the creek.  Due to the rugged, mountainous terrain, locations upstream of Rock Branch Rd were inaccessible by the survey team.

Time range is approximated from video timestamp. What likely began as a waterspout moving toward the south-southwest over the tidal Patapsco River moved onshore along Cox Creek in the Riviera Beach area of northeastern Anne Arundel County. A grill was flipped and numerous trees were snapped near the top, falling in a convergent manner near the intersection of|Waterview Drive and Riverside Drive.||The tornado continued toward the south, where a street sign was bent and large sections of siding were removed from a house near the intersection of Waterview Drive and Hilltop Road; numerous trees were downed in a convergent manner on this block, as well. Large tree limbs and tree tops were snapped near the intersection of West End Drive and Park Place, with additional large limbs twisted off and tops of trees sheared off near the intersection of West End Drive and Fieldstone Place.||The tornado then crossed Stoney Creek near the bridge on MD-173 Fort Smallwood Road, before felling additional trees and a power pole prior to dissipating in the Sunset Beach area.

A tornado descended around Patapsco Road where a few trees were uprooted and snapped. As the tornado tracked through New York Avenue and Magothy Road, the intensity of the wind increased with numerous trees uprooted along with a power pole and several tree trunks snapped. A boat was also lofted into the air, over a pier,|and onto a jet ski. Damage was laying in different directions, indicative of rotation. A large tree also fell onto a house. Another home off Magothy Road had roof singles ripped off, along with a loss of some siding.||The tornado tracked over Grays Creek, and more trees were uprooted along Dobbins Lane. Numerous trees were uprooted along Edgewater Road with damage facing different directions. A few tree trunks were snapped as well. A security camera near Edgewater Road recorded the swirling winds passing through.||Based on data from the FAA BWI Terminal Doppler Weather Radar, the tornado continued across the Magothy River, moving onshore in Cape St. Claire just east of Persimmon Point. Damage consisting of snapped and uprooted trees was observed along River Bay Road and in the vicinity of Broadview Drive and Saint Catherine Drive. Here, an eyewitness observed dust and debris that had been lofted into the air. The tornado lifted near this area, prior to the mouth of the Little Magothy River, as radar data showed it being undercut by outflow associated with the storm that had previously spawned another tornado. No additional damage has been reported to the east of this point.

NWS storm survey found the path of a brief, weak tornado near Lake Santeetlah. The first damage was observed from a distance on a ridge near Funnel Top Mountain where several trees were blown down. The tornado traveled south/southwest and crossed Highway 143, downing trees along the road. Additional trees were downed along a trail just east of Snowbird Mountain Lodge. The path was sporadic with just some limbs down as the tornado continued south/southwest, with additional trees downed along Old Santeetlah Road and W Buffalo Rd where the path ended near the intersection of Boomer Rd.
